text: This chapter's three ideas — design, build, and navigate — come together in one worked scenario: a small Equipment Checkout application for the IT department, planned the way a real ServiceNow developer would plan it, start to finish.

Two real entities, and the same decision rule from Lesson 24 applied fresh. A checkout is one employee's specific request to take a piece of equipment out for a window of time — it needs to be approved, tracked while it's out, and closed out when it's returned, so it extends task, inheriting state and an assignment group for the equipment pool. The equipment item itself has no workflow at all — it's descriptive inventory data that just exists, so it stands alone with no parent, the same reasoning Lesson 24 used for a simple lookup table.

Building follows Lesson 25's sequence exactly. The checkout table gets an equipment_item reference field pointing at the equipment table, plus a requested_for reference to sys_user, since the person submitting a checkout isn't always the person it's for. Form Layout splits into a Request section and a Logistics section; List Layout surfaces short_description, equipment_item, and state, so the coordinator managing the pool can scan open checkouts at a glance.

The Application Menu for Equipment Checkout already exists the moment the scoped app does — nothing new to build there. Closing the real reachability gap from Lesson 25 takes two modules, both pointing at that same menu. Checkouts, List of Records against the checkout table, gets Order 100 so it's the first thing the coordinator sees. Equipment Catalog, also List of Records, gets Order 200, sitting beneath it since it's reached far less often.

Entities identified, the extend decision made correctly for each, the reference field and both layouts built, and two ordered modules closing the reachability gap — that's the full real sequence behind any custom application in this chapter. Chapter 7 moves past the navigator entirely, starting with Lesson 28's GlideDialogWindow and GlideModal.
